extracted.intended_audience: fiction and creative writers (especially narrative prose writers and workshop participants)
extracted.subtask_description: A glossary-style set of craft definitions and short prescriptive guidelines for fiction writers covering grammar, syntax, figures of speech, voice, and workshop practice. Useful as reference guidance for producing and critiquing narrative prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism vs. critique (word choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: criticize and criticism have gathered a negative charge, while critique and critiquing still sound neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer neutral terms (critique/critiquing) when engaging in constructive evaluation; be aware of connotations when choosing your vocabulary for feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dingbat (typographic device)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dingbat is a little figure or device used to decorate or emphasize a break in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize dingbats as decorative devices; use them to emphasize breaks when appropriate. (Example shown in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded clause
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term included as a reference; understand embedded clauses as subordinate structures within sentences (implied guidance elsewhere in the manual).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar (knowledge and wise rule-breaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental system of a language; the rules for using words so they make sense. People can have good grammatical sense without knowing the rules, but to break the rules wisely, you have to know the rules well. Knowledge is freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn grammatical rules thoroughly so that any departures are deliberate and effective; grammatical knowledge is enabling, not merely prescriptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor (use and pitfalls)
rubrics_metrics.description: An implied comparison or description: instead of saying A is like B, you say A is B, or you use B to refer to A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphor widely—much language is metaphorical—but watch for common, dead metaphors and for mixed metaphors (these can produce grotesque, unintended effects). Examples and comparisons (metaphor vs simile) provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: A regular rhythm or beat. If prose develops meter for more than a few words in a row, it stops being prose and turns into poetry, whether you want it to or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unintentionally imposing a steady metrical pattern across prose; be mindful of rhythm so that prose retains its intended form and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mot juste (the right word)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for precise word choice—select the word that best fits meaning, tone, and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onomatopoeia
rubrics_metrics.description: A word that sounds like what it means (e.g., sizzle, hiss, slurp).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use onomatopoeic words when sound-evocation enhances the scene, but avoid overuse or forced examples that draw attention away from the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of speech (functional awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes of words, determined by their use in the sentence, such as noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, adjective, preposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the parts of speech because they are necessary vocabulary for discussing and understanding grammar; this knowledge aids both writing and critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathetic fallacy (caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A phrase used (often condescendingly) to describe a passage of writing in which the landscape, weather, and other things mirror or embody human emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about literal personification of landscape/emotions; use environmental mirroring deliberately rather than as cliché.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer group (workshop practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of writers who meet regularly to read and discuss one another’s writing, forming a leaderless workshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular peer groups/workshops are a practical way to get feedback and develop craft; participate in leaderless groups for mutual critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person (of the verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: The English verb has six persons, three in the singular and three in the plural (examples given for regular and irregular verbs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand verb person forms (first, second, third; singular/plural) so you can use tense and agreement correctly in narration and dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence fragment (use and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of sentence used in place of a whole sentence. A fragment lacks either the subject or the predicate or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally avoid sentence fragments in writing unless the omitted elements are clearly implied by context; fragments occur naturally in speech and can be used for effect, but repeated fragments in narrative tend to sound awkward or affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simile (explicit comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comparison using like or as; the comparison is made openly in simile, whereas in metaphor the like or as disappears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose between simile and metaphor based on desired directness or subtlety of comparison; be aware of the rhetorical difference and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream-of-consciousness (mode and constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fictional mode/voice in which the reader participates in the moment-to-moment experience, reactions, and thoughts of the viewpoint character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stream-of-consciousness in passages or short pieces where appropriate; avoid sustaining it throughout a whole novel except with careful intent, as it is constrictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax (arrangement of words)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrangement of words (in their appropriate forms) by which their connexion and relation in a sentence are shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train yourself to 'hear' or 'feel' syntax so you can detect tangled or clear sentences; diagramming sentences can be enlightening and strengthen your sense of sentence structure—syntax is essential equipment for narrative prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenses (verb time forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The forms of a verb that indicate the times at which the action is supposed to be happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious of tense choices and their narrative effects; verb forms establish temporal relationships and narrative perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing dead metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: One thing writers have to watch for is the common, dead metaphors, which when mixed come dreadfully alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid combining stale clichés and overused metaphors; mixing them can produce awkward or unintentionally humorous results—revive or replace cliché with fresh imagery.
